item.title: Why Do People Love Canned Cocktails?
item.description:
Consumer Behavior

Why Do People Love Canned Cocktails?

Consumers want a cocktail, but not their parents’ kind of cocktail.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Many of today's consumers think of cocktails as less of a ritual and more as an everyday-life experience.
  • Consumers want products that are new and different, but not too different.
  • The canned cocktail fits with the idea that consumers crave affordable luxury.

Once upon a time, being offered a cocktail in a can would have seemed like an insult. Cocktails were supposed to be shaken, stirred, garnished, and served in an appropriate glass. A can was reserved for cheaper drinks on the go, such as beer, soda, or perhaps the alcopops of the 1990s. Yet canned cocktails have moved decisively into the mainstream. In the United States, canned and ready-to-drink cocktails are now a substantial category, with consumers increasingly choosing canned margaritas, espresso martinis, negronis, and spritzes (Financial Times, 2026).

Eliminating Effort

How has this change happened? For one, their popularity reflects a broader change in how consumers think about drinking: less as a ritual that requires effort and more as an experience that should fit seamlessly into everyday life. The most obvious appeal of a canned cocktail is that there is almost nothing to do. Open the can, and the drink is ready. That sounds trivial, but eliminating small amounts of effort can substantially change how consumers approach a product. A traditional cocktail requires ingredients, equipment, ice, measurements, and some knowledge of how to combine them. Even ordering one in a bar involves waiting. A canned cocktail removes virtually all of these steps. Importantly, this convenience makes canned cocktails seem almost like an accessory that can be taken to many different places and occasions. Take a picnic. A bottle of gin, tonic, ice, glasses, and garnishes are possible, but hardly convenient. A can is much easier to put into a bag and take outside. The same applies to festivals, barbecues, beaches, parks, and other informal occasions.

Another reason for canned cocktails being in demand is that consumers want products that are new and different, but not too different. They want a drink they’re familiar with and know the taste of, but want to have it in a way that’s different and new. They also want to signal that they’re different from previous generations of drinkers who had to choose between convenience (think canned beer) and sophistication (think a cocktail mixed by a knowledgeable bartender). Now, consumers can have both the convenience and the sophistication, without being too different to be unrecognizable as a cool and culturally relevant product. Research shows that consumers want exactly that (Chan et al, 2012): They want a distinct product that is different from the mainstream, but not so different that no one would recognize it. In other words, we want to be seen drinking something smart and special, with a twist.

Affordable Luxury

Finally, the canned cocktail fits with the idea that consumers crave affordable luxury (Mundel et al., 2017). A cocktail at a bar can easily cost $20 or more, whereas a supermarket can may cost only a few dollars. This does not make canned cocktails cheap in absolute terms, but it makes the cocktail experience much more affordable. Given recent trends of inflation and increased cost of living, consumers want flexibility around drinking. They may drink at home before going out, have one drink at a barbecue, take something to a festival, or enjoy a drink outdoors. Canned cocktails can accompany all of these occasions while being affordable.

So are canned cocktails just another alcohol fad? The trends above suggest otherwise. Canned cocktails reflect a broader consumer desire for affordable products that offer a special experience.

item.title: How to Do More With Less
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

How to Do More With Less

Everything is getting cut down. So what can you do?

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Budgets are falling.
  • Expectations are rising.
  • There are ways to keep up with rising expectations on lower budgets.

I just got off a project that was told to do more with less. The realization didn’t come at first. The leader delivered the news well. There was no spin, no jargon, no softening the blow.

She said the number. Immediately, everyone was thinking: We're going to have to do more with less. She then said she knew it was hard and that it was unexpected. She said she had faith in the team and that they would figure it out.

But a 40 percent cut? That’s rough. Even for the best teams.

And then, over the next three weeks, that team worked silently to rebuild the exact same plan they'd run the year before, just smaller.

Nobody invented anything. Nobody got creative. Everyone played it safe. I've seen this happen enough times that I stopped thinking of it as a fluke.

Yet something very interesting happens from time to time. Some teams get cut and come back with the best work they've ever done. They use the challenge to deliver some of the best work they have ever done because it forces a clarity that only a cut can introduce.

So what separates the teams that thrive under budget pressure from the ones that succumb to the weight? Here are three battle-tested real-world creative tools you can use the next time you are faced with a budget cut.

1. Name the Tradeoff

Unless we are willing to accept that the budget cut brings in a necessary pruning, we are fighting against the inevitable.1 So instead, say the scary part out loud. Say out loud what you are choosing to give up.

It feels like admitting failure. And it’s uncomfortable. But this is not admitting failure.

What you're actually doing is handing your team permission to lose something, and in that permission to lose is what unlocks the ability to rebuild.2 Surprisingly, this step sparks creativity3 in the team.

I worked one time with a meeting director who did this in a room I was standing in. She named the three things her group was going to stop doing as a result of the cut, by name, right there in front of everyone.

The strange thing was that you could feel the temperature in the room change. Half the people who had been carrying those three burdens for months felt immediately relieved and were now free to get creative about another portion of the event.

2. Cut the List to One

Scarcity is going to narrow down the attention to one thing only.4 And that is super-helpful when it comes to how to do more with less. When facing cuts, naming the trade-off is necessary. And the immediate follow-up is that you now have to cut the list to one most important thing.

People in the organization tend to resist this cut because narrowing to one feels reckless. It feels irresponsible. It's almost perceived as a rash decision, one that is made without carefully considering other options that often yield more than one result.

Yet the truth is that cutting the list down to one is the exact opposite.5 The reckless or irresponsible version is asking for six things with the resources for one and letting everyone go off and choose which five to fail at.

When we cut the list down to one, we narrow down the essentials of the cut and offer the opportunity for responsibility on that selection. That responsibility creates ownership, and that usually leads to the list being cut down to the most important compromise.

3. Practice Constraint Before It Rears Its Ugly Head

This is one of the key differentiators between teams that thrive under budget cut pressure and the ones who collapse under such pressure. It’s practicing the inevitable.6

If every budget grew every time, we would be living in a fantasy land. Sometimes budgets go up, sometimes they come down. Practicing for the inevitability is just a good creative pathway.

What I do to help inspire teams to practice the constraint is to make an artificial one within the team. Not when it is necessary, and not waiting for something to be broken. It’s all about making the proactive choice7 to play within a smaller box.

Take the next project and shave off 20 percent and see if the team can still thrive. Take the next quarter and trim 15 percent. Proactively.

Even individual team members can do this practice routine to get in shape for the eventuality that there will be a cut at some point. And they will be ready to go with creative and innovative solutions from the get-go.

At the end of the day, if you're leading a team through less right now, here's one sentence to say tomorrow that can change everything and unlock creative solutions8: OK, so here's the one thing we have to get right this year, and here's what we're letting go of to do it.

What is often missing is somebody willing to stand up and say what matters now, and what doesn't anymore. And that one statement can unlock potential that will allow your team to thrive under budget pressure.

item.title: 6 Reasons to Avoid Using AI in Coercive Control Legal Cases
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

6 Reasons to Avoid Using AI in Coercive Control Legal Cases

Artificial intelligence poses risks in domestic violence data analysis.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Both sides increasingly use artificial intelligence to analyze communications in domestic violence cases.
  • Pitfalls include low-context analysis, pattern hallucination, bias, the streetlight effect and data exposure.
  • While AI analysis is easy and profitable for some, it can distort domestic violence legal cases.
  • Patterns that are detectable in written texts are not the full scope of the abuse.

By Chitra Raghavan, Ph.D., and Lisa Aronson Fontes, Ph.D.

Both sides in contentious family court cases increasingly turn to artificial intelligence to analyze diaries and communications with former partners for evidence of abuse. Many then try to use these AI-generated analyses in court proceedings. But is it “expert evidence?”

As coercive control scholars, who also serve as expert witnesses in legal cases, we see potential pitfalls. (We'll save discussion of the advantages for another piece.)

Source: Tara Winstead / Pexels

We're concerned with the growing tendency to treat AI as an authoritative source for determining “what’s really happening" in domestic violence cases. In practice, this often involves uploading digital records—such as text messages, emails, or parenting app exchanges—to a large language model such as Claude or ChatGPT and asking it to identify abuse patterns or relationship dynamics.

Six pitfalls.

  1. Low Context Analysis

AI analysis lacks context.

Domestic abusers use coercive control to dominate their victims. Tactics can include strategic love-like acts, intimidation, isolation, monitoring, and physical, verbal, sexual, financial, and litigation abuse. Over time, control often becomes subtle, with victims responding to cues shaped by shared history.

This variability makes coercive control difficult to detect without understanding the broader relationship context, power dynamics, and behavioral patterns. AI analyzes data with only the context that it is provided. AI cannot address gestures, tone of voice, facial expression, historical context, or impact.

An example text could be, “I’m picking up the kids at your house on Friday at 5 pm. Have them ready, please.”

AI cannot see whether that statement is helpful, neutral, or problematic. Is it a welcome reminder of an unproblematic schedule change? Would the writer showing up at the receiver's house violate a protective order? Does the message push the receiver to leave work early, which is part of a pattern of interfering with their employment? Does the message fail to acknowledge that the children will be at summer camp until Sunday, or need to be picked up at 9 am on Friday because school is cancelled?

Even when digital data (such as a text or email) is available, it may lack important context.

  1. Pattern Hallucination or Algorithmic Confirmation Bias

AI will find patterns even when the data is meaningless. It may label normal relationship disagreements or assertive communication as “coercive,” producing false positives. Conversely, genuinely coercive behavior may go undetected. AI is trained to identify patterns that match specified criteria, not to determine whether those patterns mean anything in real life. As a result, AI can mistake random, coincidental, or context-dependent variations—such as angry texts between partners—for meaningful signs of abuse.

3. Mistaking Inputter Bias as Truth

The person setting the AI search criteria may knowingly or unknowingly bias the results toward a desired conclusion. Because the results “come from AI,” judges or others may perceive them as impartial. But the results are only as accurate as the rules and data entered.

AI may also identify patterns that technically fit the criteria but are meaningless. Arbitrary, biased, or flawed rules can produce misleading patterns. Users may mistakenly believe that AI has “proven” the existence of coercive control.

  1. Missing Unusual Presentations

AI cannot accurately analyze unfamiliar material. The dataset that the learning model was trained on may have been overly narrow.

For example, most coercively controlling abusers will push their partners into having sex when they don’t want to. But less commonly, abusers control their partners through sexual rejection. For survivors, this rejection can be a signal that they are “in trouble.” They may believe that resuming sexual activity will increase their safety. AI might mistakenly interpret the victim’s repeated texted attempts to initiate sex as sexual aggression, while overlooking that the abuser’s calculated rejection may itself be a form of coercive control.

  1. The Streetlight Effect, or the Available Data Bias

AI searches for patterns using only the data provided. Entire categories of abuse are invisible.

The streetlight effect refers to the observational bias of looking for information only where it’s most easily available. It’s also called the "drunkard’s search,” based on a parable about a drunk person looking for a key under the streetlight even though he knows he lost it elsewhere, because it’s easiest to see under the streetlight.

It’s easy to feed digital data such as written communications into AI. These are not necessarily where the most meaningful coercive control exists.

AI cannot measure the tone of someone’s voice, patterns of isolation, complex economic manipulation, facial expressions, environmental control, the pressure of someone’s grip, or their degree of insistence around sexual acts. Much sophisticated coercive control leaves no digital footprint. The unrecorded aspects of personal life will remain unseen.

Victims already censor their communications to avoid angering abusers. And abusers often tone down their responses on the advice of their attorneys. Furthermore, domestic abusers can use built-in or separate tools to shape their communication on parenting apps before hitting “send.”

We’ve both seen domestic abusers use parenting apps to manufacture "evidence" that the victim was abusive, while continuing to abuse the victim in other ways that were harder to document.

  1. Data Exposure

Victim-survivors (and their attorneys and paralegals) are uploading diaries, texts, and case files into AI apps with no thought about where that data goes. Depending on the product, the data can be retained, used to train future models, and reviewed by human contractors. For someone whose safety depends on an unlisted address or a sealed record, this could be a real risk.

The National Network to End Domestic Violence notes that AI users’ searches and even deleted chats may be discoverable in legal cases. Some domestic violence-focused applications, such as AimeeSays, default to greater privacy but cannot promise full protection in legal cases.

The Lure of AI in Domestic Violence Cases

Why do victim-survivors (and their coaches and attorneys) so often rely on AI in legal cases?

It’s easy. It looks impressive. It’s profitable. It’s relatively easy to gather digital data, feed it into a computer app for this purpose, and emerge with a chart that classifies thousands of messages into searchable categories. AI can count and sort the use of certain phrases and produce numbers that have an aura of statistical validity to reports. AI produces impressive-sounding categories that seem to bring order to the chaos of an abusive relationship. Many entrepreneurs sell related apps. And some coaches and experts charge top dollar to produce AI-generated reports.

People overly trust AI-generated data. AI finds patterns based on the rules it's given. People may assume those patterns are objective, reliable, or meaningful simply because they come from a computer. They fail to understand that AI is just detecting patterns based on a set of rules. This can lead to legal or psychological conclusions based on misleading patterns or flawed criteria. Conversely, AI could miss crucial power imbalances.

In summary, AI can lead to false conclusions about domestic violence. In the worst-case scenario, one might mistake “what AI found in texts” for the full scope of the alleged abuse. This could have life-changing consequences for domestic violence victim-survivors and their children.

item.title: How to Survive a Road Trip Vacation With Your Spouse
item.description:
Relationships

How to Survive a Road Trip Vacation With Your Spouse

Road trips often put the resilience of the relationship to the test.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Road trip vacations can challenge couple relationships or bring couples together.
  • Hidden strains in the couple relationship can surface with the intense time together.
  • You need to plan in advance to avoid conflict.

As a marriage counselor, I often ask couples, as a diagnostic tool, if the problems that brought them to therapy get better or worse when they’re on vacation. Best-case scenario: When they are away from the demands of the home, the dishes in the sink, the laundry to be done, the bills in the mail, and the in-laws, the stars align, and they remember why they love each other.

Worst-case scenario: They’re trapped in a car for 10 days driving from place to place in Newfoundland, in and out of hotels every two nights. All the bickering, feeling controlled, trouble with decision-making, misaligned comfort with spending, differences in values, and previously hidden competitiveness boils over like a too-full pot of stew bubbling on the stove. A mess to clean up!

A road trip means that there are countless decisions to be made. Someone had to start work months before to book the flights and hotels, rent the car, and organize who would take care of the dog. The organizer is vulnerable to the disapproval of the other partner in case any of those plans don’t turn out well.

Happy Couple in Car
Source: Fast-Stock / Shutterstock

Once you’re on the road, there’s likely to be constant disagreements about the windows being open or closed, the AC on or off, stopping or not to go pee (again), pushing to make the next destination before dinner or meandering around to visit all the craft shops en route. One partner wants to loosen the purse strings and order the lobster. The other is nervous about every penny spent and wants to share an order of fish and chips!

On the road, one driver carefully heeds the speed limit. The other believes that 10 mph above is perfectly fine, so there’s a lot of trying to coerce the other to speed up or slow down. The one at the wheel is the driver; the other is the "naggagator"! Not to mention, it’s Newfoundland, so you have to constantly keep your eye out for moose on the road!

Uncovering the Bare-Bones Dynamic

A road trip uncovers the bare-bones dynamic between the couple. Conflict often arises when one person feels strongly about how things should go, and the other feels controlled and squirms at being told what to do. This dynamic existed at home, but there, it’s diffused. You don’t have to make several decisions in the course of each hour, and you have the space to walk away, do something else, or talk it through with a friend to get some relief.

Here on the road, the stakes are high. This is your one precious vacation, and you really want it to be great! You’re spending a lot of money. You want to have fun and connect, so if things are tense, it’s magnified.

And then there’s the issue of sex. Many people think of vacations as an opportunity to enjoy sex together, so if there’ve been some struggles around sex, the fact that it’s not happening can turn the cabin of the car into a pressure cooker.

Suggestions for a Positive Trip

Ideally, your road trip will be 10 relaxed, fun days, away from the demands of everyday life, where you can hold hands and connect physically, enjoy new experiences, eat good food, connect with the magical landscape, and be flexible enough to roll with whatever pops up. It will be a chance to re-affirm your bond and create happy memories. I’d suggest you prime your expectations by actually verbalizing that wish before you head on the road. Make a pledge to each other to be easy-going, flexible, and positive, as best as possible.

Other suggestions:

  • Plan the trip together. Discuss in advance where you want to go, what you’d like to do, and what hotels to book.
  • Before you leave, talk about how to handle money. Who pays for what? Separate checks? Are you hoping to stick to a tight budget or relax a bit to be open to add-ons, outings, or boat tours that add to the cost? Get that tense conversation over with before you get the suitcases up from the basement.
  • Decide if you want to get away from it all or use the dedicated time in the car to discuss issues and problems that need sorting out. You don’t want to feel trapped in the car, forced to discuss whether to put mom in an assisted living apartment when you’re desperate to get away from that painful choice just for a few days.
  • Be aware if your partner is constantly trying to wrest your attention away from your phone. Put your phone down!
  • Discuss to what extent one or both of you will be working even though you’re on vacation. Agree about that.
  • No blaming!
  • Look for opportunities to experience things together, what John Gottman, the couple researcher, calls “turning toward your partner, rather than away.”
  • Be open to suggestions from the other—if they want you to slow down, do what John Gottman calls “permitting influence.”
  • It’s healthy if you or your partner need time alone. Don’t take it as a rejection. Let them.

Have a great time on your vacation! And don’t forget to watch out for the moose!

item.title: Overparenting: When Giving Is Really a Form of Taking
item.description:
Parenting

Overparenting: When Giving Is Really a Form of Taking

Care becomes control when used to secure validation, dependence, or possession.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Parenting undermines children’s development when support exceeds what they actually need while maturing.
  • Healthy parenting supports autonomy through perspective-taking and allowing age-appropriate choice.
  • Children can stay connected to parents without needing to remain dependent and compliant.

I recently rewatched Disney’s Tangled and had some difficulty articulating exactly why Mother Gothel was so evil and not a remarkably devoted parent. While she does keep Rapunzel in a tower, she does so to protect Rapunzel from a dangerous world. She feeds her, shelters her, and attends to her needs. Rapunzel, meanwhile, can be easily described as a rebellious teenager who ignores her mother, leaves home, and pursues excitement despite being explicitly warned not to.

Through that lens, Mother Gothel can almost look like the “giver” and Rapunzel the ungrateful “taker” in their relationship… except for one thing that gives it all away. Mother Gothel “protects” Rapunzel, not for Rapunzel’s sake, but for her own.

Mother Gothel’s care has a hidden condition. Rapunzel must remain hers. Her independence is not something Mother Gothel wants to cultivate; it threatens the very arrangement that Mother Gothel needs to preserve. Rapunzel’s magical hair keeps Mother Gothel young.

The problem is not that she benefits from taking care of Rapunzel. People normally benefit from loving relationships. The problem is that Rapunzel’s continued dependence is necessary for Mother Gothel to keep getting what she wants from the relationship.

When Care Stops Relating to the Other Person’s Needs

Mother Gothel is an extreme case, but one can see through her actions what happens when parental care becomes misaligned with what a child needs developmentally.

Researchers commonly describe this as overparenting or helicopter parenting. Parents continue to be involved in areas children should be increasingly capable of navigating themselves. They inappropriately intervene in conflicts, solve problems, alleviate manageable difficulties, or provide help that is no longer necessary.

A systematic review of 74 studies found that overparenting was predominantly associated with poorer outcomes across psychological, behavioral, social and relational, academic, and career domains among emerging adults. The overall pattern suggests that more parental involvement is not necessarily better. Also, how one gets involved is as important as how much.

Consider what can happen when a child comes home crying because someone was mean to him and a parent replies, “You don’t need anyone else. I’m always here for you.” The statement might seem wonderfully reassuring. However, this type of reassurance can become isolating. “I am here for you” is different from “You don’t need anyone else.”

Alternatively, think about when a child rejects a parent’s suggestion and hears, “I know what’s best for you.” Sometimes parents do know better. Yet there is a difference between setting limits and refusing to recognize a child’s ability to make decisions – and learn from them – on their own.

Then there is the familiar: “After everything I’ve done for you…” This statement turns offering care into creating a debt. “I cared for you because you needed me” becomes “Because I cared for you, you now owe me.” Don’t get me wrong. Gratitude is a virtue worth cultivating, but it is a problem when care becomes leverage.

When Children Become a Source of Parents' Self-Worth

Controlling care does not necessarily come from uncaring parents. In many cases, the parent genuinely loves the child, but their giving is doing two jobs at the same time: caring for the child while also helping the parent obtain something they want, such as validation, closeness, or reassurance that they matter.

In a 2024 study, Yena Kyeong and Cecilia Cheung examined mothers’ child-based self-worth in three areas: virtue, academic competence, and physical appearance. Mothers whose self-worth was more strongly based on their adolescent children’s virtue and physical appearance reported greater use of psychological control. Mothers whose self-worth depended more strongly on their children’s physical appearance also reported less autonomy-supportive parenting.

That does not mean parents should stop feeling proud of their children or stop feeling good about themselves when their children are doing well. Rather, it means that we must be careful that our good feelings are side-effects and not the main motivations for our parenting choices.

Healthy Giving Doesn’t Require Being Impersonal

None of this means parenting must be selfless or laissez-faire. That would be both unrealistic and undesirable. Parents should derive joy, identity, meaning, and connection from raising their children. Children should learn gratitude and reciprocity. Parents should also establish boundaries, impose limits, transmit values, offer guidance, and sometimes make decisions their children dislike. The key is to recognize when parenting is autonomy-supportive and when it becomes psychologically controlling.

According to a major meta-analysis published in American Psychologist, parental autonomy support was positively associated with children’s well-being, whereas psychological control was positively associated with ill-being. Autonomy support does not mean letting children do whatever they want. It involves trying to understand their perspective, supporting age-appropriate self-expression and decision-making, and providing meaningful explanations when limits are set. Psychological control, on the other hand, attempts to shape children’s thoughts, feelings, or behavior through strategies such as guilt, contingent approval, or love withdrawal.

The difference between supporting autonomy or being controlling may matter beyond the parent-child relationship itself. A 2024 study of college students found that relational overparenting was associated with greater loneliness and social anxiety. This means that we shouldn’t only be blaming phones for creating an anxious generation. We should also be looking at ourselves.

Giving That Really Gives

The next time I watch Disney’s Tangled with my children, I will not only look to see how they might identify with Rapunzel. I will also see how I may be acting like Mother Gothel, albeit in less extreme ways.

As children grow up, we must realize when we need to change the ways that we give to them. The child who once needed us to solve a problem may now need us to watch them struggle through it. The teenager who once accepted our answers wholeheartedly might now need the freedom to question them.

Children’s growing independence does not need to feel like our diminishing importance. Our children can still remain connected to us without having to remain small for us.

item.title: Are Teens and Parents Ready for Back to School Without Cell Phones?
item.description:
Adolescence

Are Teens and Parents Ready for Back to School Without Cell Phones?

Parents play a critical role in device regulation, whether they like it or not.

Posted August 18, 2026

Collaborative Classroom Study Session No Cell Zone
Source: AI Generated

Australia, Canada, France, Israel, Spain, Sweden, Japan, Chile, Denmark, and England. These are the nations, among others, the US has joined in issuing cell phone bans in schools. A review of the research on smartphone and other mobile device bans in schools shows mixed results regarding benefits to academic progress, school engagement, bullying, and student wellbeing. There are also plenty of scholars, as well as students and parents, who have raised concerns about negative outcomes. Some report decreased wellbeing in the first year bans were implemented, feeling less safe, and increased disciplinary measures, which in the case of suspensions, restrict access to learning, thus inadvertently offsetting potential benefits.

Regardless of the opinions expressed or what the numbers show, there are more and more school systems in the US adopting cell phone ban policies, or, as our local school system in Montgomery County, MD calls it, PMD (Personal Mobile Device) Regulation. Whether you are jumping for joy, furious, or more neutral, some students are heading back to school in systems that require all PMDs be stored away, out of sight and out of use throughout the academic day—a.m. bell to p.m. dismissal bell and every minute in between. It is happening now.

As with any new policy or practice, these PMD bans will be an adjustment for faculty, students, and parents. High school students may have the strongest feelings about the loss of what some perceive to be a pseudo-bodily appendage. Students will need time to adapt. School staff will need to be steadfast with classroom enforcement. And if these policies have any chance of lasting, school administrators will need to be consistent in reinforcing expectations. Though parents cannot control any of these factors, there are some very important things they can do to make the transition to a non-PMD school day easier for all.

Acceptance Is a Distress Tolerance Skill

Acceptance is hard. It means acknowledging what is, even when we disagree, don’t appreciate what is happening, or do not want it to be as it is. When we refuse to accept the reality in a given moment, behaviors that do not align can cause conflict and greater distress. This is why acceptance is a distress tolerance skill. Students and parents will need to adhere to the school’s policies whether they like it or not. Behaving otherwise will likely bring discord, disruption, and distress.

Likewise, parents can accept their own and their teens’ feelings and opinions and express validation that they have the right to feel the way they do. When adults express their acceptance through validation, teens feel understood. This understanding allows two things to be true at once: “This policy sucks and I am going to follow it, see how it goes, and find ways to advocate for changes if, over time, there are negative effects.”

As one version of the Serenity Prayer goes, “May I have the serenity to accept the things I cannot change, the courage to change the things I can, and the wisdom to know the difference.”

Orient Your Teen With the Facts

As school gets going, be sure to read your school system's PMD policy. Once the policy has been reviewed, sit down with your teen and talk with them about it. Make sure they understand the parameters and definitions for the expectations. Will teens always comply? Likely not. But when teens are informed ahead of making choices, they are better able to make informed decisions and be accountable.

Our local school system had previously implemented some PMD restrictions throughout the academic day for middle school and only during academic classes for high school. This year, the regulation states its purpose: “To prohibit the use of personal mobile devices by Montgomery County Public Schools (MCPS) students while on MCPS property or engaged in MCPS-sponsored activities.” It defines a PMD as “any non-MCPS-issued device used to connect to the Internet and send or receive data via voice, video, or text. This includes mobile phones, e-readers, tablets, personal computers, smart watches, smart glasses or other devices equipped with microphones, headphones (including airpods/earbuds), speakers, and/or cameras.” The policy goes on to describe in greater detail where there may be exceptions, how noncompliance will be addressed, and potential consequence.

This conversation between parents and teens offers an opportunity for meaningful discussion, sharing perspectives, and a common understanding of the policy.

Do Your Part

Anticipate how you may respond when your teen initially complains about the torture of not accessing their devices at school. You may like to rant along with them, though that is likely to ramp up their emotions, making their adjustment more difficult. Go back to validating how they feel, “I know this is a really hard change and get how you feel.” Once emotions are more settled, help them accept their new reality. “The school’s policy is in place. It is important to follow the rules. Your feelings make sense and there are appropriate ways to advocate without disrupting your learning or getting in trouble.”

As parents, we are all guilty of texting our teens through the school day. Something comes up and we don’t want to forget to communicate, so we send a text in the middle of Chem class (then think, oh crap, they might be in Chem class). Parents will need to adjust by refraining from communicating with their teens during the school-day hours.

One of the best things for parents since the invention of cell phones is that we have instant access to our kids. One of the worst things about this is that we have been shaped by the constant access to feel anxious when we cannot reach them instantly. Check yourself when this anxious sense arises. It is an indication of how you have been trained rather than a sign of any danger. If you are really struggling with the urges to communicate, learn how to schedule texts for later so they arrive after dismissal. It’s a safe bet that your student will eagerly be checking to see what they have missed on their beloved cells during the bus ride home.

If your student is a repeat cell offender leading to a call from the school administrator, support the accountability, even if you also respectfully disagree. These are important experiences for teens to feel a response to their choices so they can reflect and make different decisions moving forward. If you feel there are unfair or disproportionate responses to student noncompliance, use the appropriate channels to appeal a decision or engage in other productive steps to advocate for changes. Your teens are watching.

Advocate for Change if Needed

Try not to assume the worst about such policies at their outset. As with anything, there will be pros and cons. A thoughtful cost-benefit analysis over time will reveal if changes may be warranted. If you or your teen feels strongly about the impacts of this new policy, find ways to advocate for a review and possible revisions. This is a great opportunity to support your teen while teaching responsible civic engagement. Maybe they want to get involved in school government, write a letter to the administration, attend a school board meeting, or start and promote a petition. The experience of hard work, impassioned and respectful dissent, and delayed gratification are terrific life skills. They will also help shape a generation of future leaders charged with finding reasonable solutions to the complex new realities of a burgeoning technological industry.
